description:
The internet in slow motion: what happens when you type a URL and press Enter. On a fast connection, a web page can appear in under half a second. This video stretches that half second across ten minutes and follows one request the whole way: the key press, DNS, the TCP handshake, HTTPS/TLS encryption, Wi-Fi, fiber optics and routers, CDNs, the server, and how the browser renders the page.
It's also a visual walkthrough of the classic interview question "what happens when you type a URL and press Enter?", using wikipedia.org and a clock taken from one real, measured page load.

The clock on screen follows that load of wikipedia.org on a fast home connection (November 2026), rounded. It starts when the browser receives the key press. It is a good case, not a typical one: plenty of pages take a second or more.

Packets come back, and the browser renders the page
The whole page load at real speed

howMade: Visuals: animation rendered in code (React and Remotion). No filmed or stock footage.
Narration: an AI voice. Music: AI-generated (Suno). Sound effects: synthesized in code.
Every figure is checked against the sources below. Where a number could not be confirmed, the script stays loose on purpose.
Found a mistake? Leave a comment and it will be checked against a source.

blocks.text: Nothing in the narration now depends on an unconfirmed figure. These points are worded loosely on purpose:

items: **Keyboard timing.** No number is spoken. One technical write-up gives 8–10 ms between checks and 15–60 ms from the start of a key press to the USB message ([Dan Luu: keyboard latency](https://danluu.com/keyboard-latency/)), but the USB specification itself was not read.
**When the first pixels appear.** No number is spoken or shown; the script says "less than half a second".

**Chrome adding `https`.** Stated without a version or date. The news reports ([XDA](https://www.xda-developers.com/google-chrome-default-https-version-90/), [9to5Google](https://9to5google.com/2021/01/11/google-chrome-address-bar-may-soon-default-to-https/)) were read; the original [Chromium blog post](https://blog.chromium.org/2021/03/) was not.

research.title: Added in the final check (16 November 2026)

items: **"Less than a millisecond" for a remembered name:** measured here. Sixty repeat lookups of `wikipedia.org` through the operating system took a median of 0.39 ms, all under 1 ms. The 3–5 ms in the table above came from a tool that adds its own start-up time.

**The failed-lookup example:** the card now shows `ww.wikipedia.org`, which returned "no such name" when checked. The earlier example, `wikipedai.org`, is a registered misspelling that redirects to Wikipedia, so it would not have produced the error.
**"Dozens more files"** became "Often dozens more files", and the caption "often dozens more requests", because this particular page needed only 5 requests.
Typing `wikipedia.org` really gets a redirect first (`301` to `www.wikipedia.org`), one extra round trip that the video skips; it shows a single request answered with `200`.

"The operating system hands that number": `0x28` is the keyboard's USB code. The operating system converts it into its own key event before any program sees it; the picture keeps `0x28` so one number can be followed from key to browser.

blocks.text: Fine to keep, worth knowing if a commenter raises them.

items: The script says the third handshake message proves to the server that it was heard. That is true, but RFC 9293 gives the main purpose as stopping old, duplicated connection attempts from causing confusion.
"Then it asks the operating system": Chrome often skips the operating system and sends the question to the resolver with its own built-in client.
Built-in laptop keyboards are often not USB and are not polled this way.
Newer connections (HTTP/3 over QUIC) merge the handshake and the encryption setup into one step.
The request is described as "a few lines of text". Modern connections (HTTP/2, which this load used) send the same information in a compact binary form.
Wikipedia runs its own caching sites and does not rent a commercial network; the "copy near you" point still holds.
The address check in S1 is simplified; browsers also consult history, a list of known suffixes and a list of sites that must use HTTPS.

narration.name: Cold open
paragraphs: You press Enter.
On a fast connection, a web page can appear in less than half a second.

In that time, your computer asked a chain of strangers for directions. It introduced itself to a machine it has never met. The two of them agreed on a secret code, out loud, in front of everyone, and nobody listening could work it out. Then a pulse of light carried your request under the street.
All of it, in about the time of one slow blink.
So let's slow time down. One blink, stretched across ten minutes. This is everything that happens when you press Enter.

narration.name: The key
paragraphs: It starts under the Enter key. Two contacts touch. A circuit closes, and a tiny chip inside the keyboard notices. It doesn't send the word "Enter". It sends a number.
A USB keyboard doesn't speak until it's spoken to. Many times a second, your computer asks it: anything new? This time, the answer is yes.
The operating system hands that number to whichever window is in front: your browser. And this is where we start the clock.
Zero milliseconds. The browser's first job is surprisingly basic. It has to work out what you meant. Is "wikipedia dot org" an address, or something to search for?
It has a dot. It has no spaces. It looks like an address. So the browser adds the part you didn't type, H-T-T-P-S, and gets ready to go.
There's just one problem.

narration.name: Finding the address: DNS
paragraphs: Your computer has no idea where Wikipedia is.
Names are for humans. Machines find each other with numbers, called IP addresses. So before anything else, the name has to become a number.
First the browser checks its own memory. Have I been here recently? Then it asks the operating system. If either one remembers, this step takes less than a millisecond. Let's say they don't.
So your computer asks a stranger: a server called a resolver, usually run by your internet provider. And if the resolver doesn't know either, it goes on a chase.

It starts at the top, with a root server. The root doesn't know where Wikipedia is, but it knows who handles every name ending in dot org. So the resolver asks them. The dot org servers don't have the answer either, but they know which server is in charge of Wikipedia's name. The resolver asks that one.
And finally, a number comes back.
Four strangers. Three of them said "not me, try over there".

That full chase is the slow path. It can take a tenth of a second, sometimes half a second. So everyone along the way keeps notes. For a popular site, the resolver already has the answer, and your number comes back in one short round trip.
When this step fails, you've seen the result. "This site can't be reached." That's the internet telling you: I asked everyone, and nobody knows that name.

narration.name: The handshake: TCP
paragraphs: Thirty milliseconds.

Now your computer has a number. But it can't just start shouting data at it. The internet is unreliable. Messages get lost, duplicated, delivered in the wrong order. So first, the two machines make a deal.
Your computer sends one tiny message: can you hear me?
The server replies: I hear you. Can you hear me?
And your computer answers: I hear you too.
Three messages. Why three, and not two?
Because after two, only your side knows the line works in both directions. The server has spoken, but it has no proof that anyone heard it. The third message is that proof.
From here on, every piece of data is numbered, so anything that goes missing can be noticed and sent again. Remember that. It matters later.

narration.name: A secret in public: TLS
paragraphs: Sixty-five milliseconds.
There's a connection. But right now, anyone along the route could read every word. The café Wi-Fi. Your internet provider. Every machine in between.
So the two sides need a secret code. And here's the puzzle: they have never met, and everything they say to each other can be overheard. How do you agree on a secret in public?
Picture paint.

You and the server openly agree on a common colour. Yellow. Everyone can see it. Then each of you secretly picks a private colour, and mixes it into the yellow. You swap the mixtures, in full view. Now each of you adds your own private colour to the mixture you received.
And you both end up with exactly the same final colour.

An eavesdropper saw the yellow, and saw both mixtures. But un-mixing paint is practically impossible. The real version uses enormous numbers instead of paint, and the idea is the same: easy to mix, almost impossible to un-mix.
One thing is still missing. How do you know this is really Wikipedia, and not an impostor?
The server shows an ID: a certificate, signed by an organisation your device already trusts. If that signature doesn't check out, you get the red warning. "Your connection is not private."
It checks out. The padlock closes. From here on, everything is scrambled.

narration.name: The trip
paragraphs: A hundred and five milliseconds.
Finally, your browser sends what you actually wanted to say. It's almost an anticlimax. A few lines of text: get me the home page.
And here's something I skipped. Every message so far, every "can you hear me", every jar of paint, made a physical journey. Let's follow this one.

It leaves your laptop as radio waves. Soon after, it becomes pulses of light in a strand of glass about as thin as a human hair. Inside that glass, your request moves at about two hundred thousand kilometres per second.
It doesn't know the route. Nothing does. It's passed from router to router, often a dozen or more, and each one knows only one thing: which neighbour is a step closer.
You might picture it diving into a cable on the ocean floor. Those cables are real, and they carry nearly all the data that moves between continents.

But your request probably never gets that far. Because the big sites worked out a trick: if the trip takes too long, shorten the trip. They keep copies of themselves in hundreds of cities around the world. Your request most likely ends in a building not far from where you're sitting.

narration.name: The server
paragraphs: A hundred and twenty-five milliseconds.
Your request arrives at a building full of machines. Hundreds of them, sometimes thousands, and it only needs one.
At the door stands a load balancer. Its whole job is to look at who's busy and point: you, take this one.
That server reads your request and gathers what it needs. Sometimes it asks a database. Sometimes it grabs a copy it prepared earlier. Then it builds the reply.
On top goes a three-digit code. Two hundred means: here you go. And if the page doesn't exist, this is the moment a 404 is born.

narration.name: The reply and the page
paragraphs: A hundred and forty milliseconds.
The reply is too big for one message. So it's chopped into packets, each holding about a paragraph of text, and each one finds its own way back.

Some arrive out of order. Some don't arrive at all. Remember the numbering from the handshake? This is what it was for. Your computer puts them back in order, and asks again for anything that's missing.

What arrives isn't a picture of a web page. It's instructions. And as the browser reads them, it discovers the job has barely started. This page needs a stylesheet. And fonts. And scripts, and images. Often dozens more files, each one a new request, and most of them make the same trip you just watched.

While they stream in, the browser builds the page in layers. First the structure: what is a heading, what is a paragraph. Then the style: colours and sizes. Then the geometry: where every box sits, down to the pixel.
And then, at last, it paints.
Less than half a second after the clock started, light leaves your screen.

narration.name: One blink
paragraphs: That took ten minutes. Here it is at real speed.
*(pause for the replay)*
Again.
*(pause for the replay)*
That was a good case: a fast connection, a copy of the site nearby, a light page. Plenty of pages take longer, a second or more. But the steps are always the same.
A circuit closing. Four strangers. Three hellos. A secret mixed in public. Light in glass. A doorman, a reply in pieces, and a page drawn in layers.
And this isn't happening once. It's happening billions of times a day, all over the world, and almost every time, it just works.
But one step in this story hides something strange. That strand of glass? The light inside it should leak out through the sides. It doesn't, and the reason is a beautiful piece of physics.
That's the next video.
